newsitem.title: FRANCE: GEC wants to keep half of Franco-British venture.
newsitem.headline: GEC wants to keep half of Franco-British venture.

text.p: General Electric Plc wants to keep a 50-percent stake in the planned combination of GEC-Alsthom Framatome and is ready to pay for it, its chairman said on Wednesday in a newspaper interview.

Lord Weinstock said that the talks about merging the industrial power and high-speed-train venture GEC-Alsthom with France's state-controlled nuclear engineering group Framatome should not change the balance of power in the Anglo-French venture with Alcatel-Alsthom.

"The operation concerns mainly the relations within GEC-Alsthom. However important it is, the balance in the company should not be changed. We should keep the same stake as Alcatel Alsthom. Not more and not less. Even if we have to pay a dowry for it," Weinstock told the Les Echos financial newspaper.
The French state in August gave its green light to the planned merger after years of opposition to Alcatel taking a majority stake in Framatome.

Alcatel has a 44 percent stake in Framatome and its chairman Serge Tchuruk has said in the past that he expected French interests -- Alcatel plus state-owned groups CEA and EDF which also have Framatome stakes -- to have a majority in the new enlarged group.
In a second phase, Tchuruk wanted to float a part of GEC-Alsthom Framatome in order to focus the venture's management on financial performance.

"Framatome is an important operation because nuclear power will become an alternative again. There are going to be new nuclear constructions programmes even though there are none at the moment. GEC Alsthom will have a good card to play with Framatome," Weinstock said.
The shareholders of Framatome are meeting today in a supervisory board meeting to nominate Dominique Vignon as chairman and chief executive, replacing Jean-Claude Leny.
Leny, who reaches retirement age at 68 in December, headed Framtome for more than 25 years and was publicly hostile to a merger with GEC Alsthom.
Vignon, currently director of nuclear activities, will have as a main task to smooth the planned merger and win over the resistance to the pending loss of independence among the 19,000 staff.
